title: Sequoyah and His Daughter Prove the Cherokee Script
text:
Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith who could neither read nor write English. He had seen white Americans read marks on paper and became convinced that his own people could have what he called talking leaves. Around 1809 he began trying to create a way of writing Cherokee. For years neighbors thought he was wasting his time, or worse, practicing witchcraft.

His first attempts used a symbol for every word, which proved unworkable. He then realized that Cherokee could be broken into a limited number of syllables. By about 1821 he had created a syllabary of some eighty-five characters, one for each sound.

According to accounts gathered by later writers, he taught the system to his young daughter, Ayoka, and the two demonstrated it to Cherokee leaders. Sequoyah was sent out of the room while the men dictated words to Ayoka, who wrote them down. Then he came back and read them aloud. Or, in other versions, the roles were reversed. Either way, the leaders were persuaded that the marks carried speech.

The script spread with astonishing speed. Because it fit the language so closely, Cherokee speakers could learn it in days. Within a few years a large part of the Cherokee Nation could read and write, and in 1828 the Cherokee Phoenix, a bilingual newspaper, began publication.
lesson: A child who learns first can help a parent prove an idea to the world. Patience in the face of mockery can turn a private project into a gift to a whole people.
location: Cherokee Nation (modern Tennessee, Alabama and Arkansas, USA)
source: Grant Foreman, Sequoyah (1938); accounts collected by later biographers and Cherokee histories
caveat: Details of the demonstration with Ayoka vary between accounts and come from later tradition.
